description: Lunasolum is developing an interactive lunar exploration and landing site assessment platform covering the Moon's entire surface. Through scientifically grounded simulations and intuitive visualizations, we aim to simplify lunar mission planning and make space exploration more accessible. Our vision is to bridge scientific precision with innovative technology, supporting the next generation of lunar exploration.
summary:
Lunasolum is an interactive lunar exploration and landing site assessment platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It simplifies the complex process of evaluating lunar landing locations by combining NASA scientific data, physics-based analysis, and immersive 3D visualization.

Built using Python, FastAPI, React, CesiumJS, and Babylon.js, Lunasolum integrates NASA SPICE ephemerides and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data to calculate Sun and Earth positions, terrain-aware illumination, direct-to-Earth visibility, and time-dependent observation windows.

Users can explore the entire Moon, select locations, examine local terrain, and evaluate changing environmental conditions. A physics-based recommendation engine screens candidate landing sites against configurable illumination and Earth-visibility requirements, providing explainable rankings without relying on fabricated predictions.

While geometric analysis supports global lunar exploration, detailed terrain-aware assessments currently focus on the available south-polar DEM coverage.

Lunasolum makes scientific lunar mission-planning concepts more accessible to researchers, students, and space enthusiasts while establishing an extensible foundation for future mission-survival simulations.
details:
1. The Problem

Selecting a suitable lunar landing site involves more than identifying a flat surface. Lunar missions must account for changing solar illumination, extreme terrain, prolonged darkness, and the availability of direct communication with Earth.

These challenges are particularly significant near the Moon's south pole, where low solar elevation angles, deep craters, and complex terrain create highly variable illumination conditions.

Although scientific tools and datasets exist, integrating astronomical calculations, lunar elevation data, and time-dependent visibility analysis can be challenging for researchers, students, and mission planners.

Lunasolum addresses this challenge by bringing scientific calculations and interactive lunar visualization together in one accessible platform.

2. Our Solution

Lunasolum is a browser-based lunar exploration and preliminary landing-site assessment application that combines NASA scientific datasets with physics-based calculations and interactive 3D visualization.

The platform allows users to:

  • Explore the Moon through an interactive CesiumJS 3D globe using NASA-derived lunar imagery and terrain.
  • Select lunar coordinates and simulation dates.
  • Calculate Sun and Earth positions relative to a selected location.
  • Examine terrain-aware solar illumination and geometric direct-to-Earth visibility.
  • Explore local lunar terrain using Babylon.js.
  • Evaluate time-dependent visibility conditions.
  • Generate physics-based recommendations for candidate landing sites.
  • Inspect scientific results, assumptions, and dataset provenance.

The application is designed to make complex lunar environmental information easier to understand without hiding the scientific limitations of its calculations.

3. Scientific Methodology

Lunasolum uses a standalone Python scientific engine built around NASA-derived astronomical and lunar terrain data.

NASA SPICE Ephemerides

NASA's SPICE toolkit provides the astronomical geometry necessary to determine Sun and Earth positions relative to locations on the lunar surface.

The scientific engine performs coordinate transformations and calculates local azimuth and elevation for selected observation times.

NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA)

LOLA digital elevation models provide measured lunar topography.

The application uses configured south-polar elevation data to construct local terrain representations and estimate how surrounding terrain obstructs sunlight and Earth visibility.

The terrain-analysis engine incorporates lunar curvature, local horizon calculations, and explicit coordinate-reference handling.

Time-Dependent Visibility

Users can evaluate visibility across selected mission intervals rather than relying on a single observation time.

The backend computes sampled illumination conditions, Earth-visibility windows, and intervals when both are simultaneously available.

Physics-Based Landing-Site Recommendations

Lunasolum includes a deterministic recommendation engine that evaluates candidate lunar locations against configurable mission conditions.

The algorithm considers:

  • Solar visibility fraction.
  • Geometric Earth visibility fraction.
  • Simultaneous Sun/Earth visibility.
  • Darkness intervals.
  • Earth-visibility outages.
  • Terrain-data availability.

Candidate locations are classified according to their compliance with the selected screening constraints and ranked using transparent, configurable weights.

Unlike a black-box prediction system, the recommendation engine provides explainable results based on the existing scientific calculations.

These recommendations are preliminary visibility-based assessments, not certifications of landing safety.

4. Technical Architecture

Lunasolum follows a modular architecture that separates scientific computation from visualization.

Scientific Backend

  • Python 3.12
  • NASA SPICE / SpiceyPy
  • NASA LOLA digital elevation models
  • NumPy and scientific geospatial processing
  • FastAPI
  • Pydantic

Frontend and Visualization

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Vite
  • CesiumJS for global lunar exploration
  • Babylon.js for local terrain visualization

Engineering and Quality Assurance

  • Git and GitHub
  • GitHub Actions CI
  • Pytest
  • Ruff
  • Mypy
  • Frontend unit and regression tests
  • Playwright browser testing

The Python scientific engine independently calculates lunar geometry and terrain visibility. FastAPI exposes these results through versioned endpoints, while the frontend presents them through interactive controls and visualizations.

This separation allows scientific functionality to be tested independently of the rendering engines.

5. What Makes Lunasolum Different?

Connecting Global Exploration With Local Scientific Analysis

Users can navigate the global Moon and transition to local terrain inspection within the same application.

Scientific Geometry Instead of Artificial Lighting

Solar geometry originates from NASA SPICE calculations rather than independently generated frontend animations.

Terrain-Aware Visibility

The application considers actual lunar elevation data and terrain horizons instead of relying exclusively on idealized spherical geometry.

Explainable Site Recommendations

Rather than displaying unexplained suitability predictions, Lunasolum evaluates candidate sites against explicit mission constraints and provides the underlying metrics.

Scientific Transparency

The interface distinguishes available measurements, calculated results, unknown conditions, dataset coverage, and modeling limitations.

Modular Engineering

The scientific engine, API, and visualization components are independently structured, allowing future expansion without replacing the entire application.

6. Scientific Accuracy and Limitations

An important design principle of Lunasolum is distinguishing between global geometric calculations and regional terrain-supported scientific analysis.

Global lunar capability: Users can explore the Moon and calculate Sun/Earth geometric positions within supported ephemeris coverage.

Detailed terrain-aware capability: Terrain-horizon analysis, local elevation rendering, and physics-based site recommendations currently depend on the available NASA LOLA south-polar DEM coverage.

Although Cesium provides global lunar terrain visualization, this does not mean that the scientific backend has independently validated terrain-aware visibility for every location on the Moon.

The current implementation also uses simplified geometric visibility models and discrete temporal sampling.

Direct-to-Earth geometric visibility is not equivalent to guaranteed radio communication.

The recommendation engine does not yet assess all landing hazards, including detailed surface roughness, boulders, regolith properties, spacecraft landing dynamics, or complete thermal and power constraints.

Therefore, Lunasolum is an educational and preliminary mission-analysis tool, not a flight-certified landing-site selection system.

7. Intended Impact

Lunasolum aims to make lunar mission-planning concepts more accessible to students, researchers, educators, and space enthusiasts.

By connecting authentic scientific datasets to interactive visualization, the platform helps users understand how lunar geography, illumination, observation time, and Earth visibility influence mission planning.

Its modular architecture also provides a foundation for further scientific and engineering development.

8. Future Development

Our long-term vision is to evolve Lunasolum into a more comprehensive lunar mission-planning and survival simulation platform.

Planned enhancements include:

  • Expanding scientifically validated DEM coverage across the Moon.
  • Improving terrain resolution and landing-hazard assessments.
  • Developing more advanced landing-site comparison and optimization.
  • Modeling solar power generation and battery state of charge.
  • Evaluating communication-link budgets and operational outages.
  • Simulating thermal conditions and spacecraft operating modes.
  • Integrating mission-survival assessment.
  • Deploying the application as a publicly accessible web platform.
